drills.title: Add up a cart
drills.prompt: Arrange the lines so the program adds up the cart and prints the total. The first two lines can go in either order. Two lines do not belong.
drills.explain: The accumulator pattern has three parts: a start value before the loop, an update inside it, and the result after it. total += p adds to what is already there, while total = p would throw the old total away. Java writes the for-each loop with a colon (for (int p : prices)), not with the word in.

drills.title: for, continue and do / while
drills.prompt: Fill the blanks so the program prints the goal output: the numbers 1 to 5 without the 3, then the number of PIN tries.
drills.explain: A for loop has three parts: where to start (i = 1), how long to keep going (i <= 5) and the step after each round (i++). continue skips the rest of this round only, while break would leave the loop completely and stop at 2. do { ... } while (...) runs its body first and checks afterwards, so the body always runs at least once.

drills.title: Skip, stop and never start
drills.prompt: Read the code and type exactly what it prints, one line per line of output.
drills.explain: continue skips only the round for n = 3. At n = 6 the break leaves the whole loop, so 6 is never printed. A while loop checks first: x < 3 is false from the start, so its body never runs. A do / while runs once before it checks, so x becomes 6.

drills.title: The total that has no start
drills.prompt: The program should add up the cart, but it does not compile. Click the line the compiler complains about, then choose the fix.
drills.explain: total += p means total = total + p, which reads total before the first round. A local variable that was never given a value cannot be read, so the compiler stops you. The start value of a sum is 0, and it belongs before the loop (a 1 would make every total too big by one).

drills.title: Review the AI's sales report
drills.prompt: An AI assistant wrote this sales report for four days of sales. It compiles and runs, but tick the real problems (there are two).

issues.text: The total leaves out the first day because the loop starts at index 1
issues.why: Indexes start at 0. Starting at 1 skips sales[0], so the total (and everything computed from it) is 1200 too small. Use int i = 0, or a for-each loop.

issues.text: average is cut to a whole number because total / sales.length divides two ints
issues.why: The decimals are dropped before the result goes into a double. Cast one side: (double) total / sales.length.

non_issues.text: best = 0 as the start value is a bug
non_issues.why: Sales are never negative, so any real sale beats 0. (For data that can be negative, start from the first item instead.)

non_issues.text: The condition i < sales.length should be i <= sales.length
non_issues.why: The last valid index is length - 1. With <= the loop would read sales[4] and crash.

non_issues.text: A for-each loop cannot be used to look for the biggest value
non_issues.why: It reads every item in turn, and an if inside it can compare and remember the best one. Only a need for the position requires the classic loop.

drills.explain: Loop reports fail quietly: the program runs and prints numbers that look reasonable. Check the first and last round of every loop, and every / between two ints.
